claims.statement: The SSE transport is a single tokio broadcast channel of capacity 100 (broadcast::channel::<SseMessage>(100)) created in server::main together with one CancellationToken; the Sender is handed to axum through AppState and to GraphQL resolvers through Schema::data, so mutations, the four upload handlers and the nested MCP HTTP service all publish onto the same bus. SseMessage is { event: String, data: String } — the JSON payload is serialized once at the sender and every subscriber receives identical bytes.

sse_send calls `let _ = tx.send(..)`, deliberately ignoring a send failure whether the channel has no receivers or is full. Progress is therefore best-effort telemetry and not a work queue: on a headless server with no browser attached every event is silently discarded, and no client-side behaviour may depend on delivery — the authoritative state is re-read from SQLite.

GET /events is served by sse_handler, which calls sse_tx.subscribe() per connection (so each client sees every event) and wraps an async_stream loop in Sse::new(..).keep_alive(KeepAlive::default()) so an idle stream keeps emitting keep-alive comments. Inside the loop a RecvError::Lagged(n) only logs a warning and continues — a slow client loses messages but keeps its connection — while RecvError::Closed and cancel.cancelled() both break the loop and end the response.

spawn_cli_action is the template for GraphQL-triggered long work: it emits {prefix}_started, then waits for WRITE_LOCK and acquires its database connection *inside* the spawned task and runs the CLI subcommand, and emits {prefix}_complete with success:true or {prefix}_error with success:false plus a human-readable message. Acquiring after `started` is what guarantees a pool-exhaustion failure surfaces as {prefix}_error instead of silence — the invariant being that every code path emits exactly one terminal event.

The event prefixes actually emitted by the web server are: sort_roms, check_roms, generate_playlists, purge_roms, convert_roms and purge_irds via spawn_cli_action; download_dats and purge inlined in the download_dats and purge_system mutations (note the system-purge prefix is `purge`, not `purge_system`); and import_dat, import_rom, import_patch and import_irds from the four multipart upload handlers, each of which returns 202 Accepted and reports only over SSE.

OxyromonMcp::run_action fans the same {prefix}_started/_complete/_error triple into the web server's broadcast channel, but only in server builds where self.sse_tx is Some (i.e. mounted at /mcp by mcp_http_service, which calls with_sse) *and* the tool passed an sse_prefix. The prefixes used are import_dats, download_dats, sort_roms, check_roms, convert_roms, purge_roms, purge and purge_irds; import_roms and set_setting pass None and therefore emit nothing to /events.

Actions differ in when they become visible on /events: run_action takes WRITE_LOCK and acquires a pooled connection *before* sending {prefix}_started, and purge_system and download_dats also take the lock first, so such an action queued behind another writer is invisible to the browser until it actually begins, whereas spawn_cli_action and the upload handlers announce {prefix}_started before waiting for the lock.

Progress-bar movement is not bridged into SSE: every GraphQL action and upload handler runs on ProgressBar::hidden() and SSE carries only lifecycle events with their message string. MCP is the only bridge — run_action creates a visible none-style bar with start_action so there is something to read, then (only when the caller passed a progressToken) spawns a poller that sleeps 400 ms, samples (position, length, message) from the subcommand-owned bar, and sends notifications/progress solely when that tuple changed, giving up when notify_progress fails and being aborted as soon as the work settles.

connect_sse opens one EventSource('/events') for the SPA's whole lifetime and leaks its closures. Because EventSource reconnects by itself but never replays missed events, it installs an onopen handler that resets every in-flight flag (purging_system_id, sorting_system_id, checking_system_id, purging_irds_system_id, generating_playlists, purging_roms, purging_game_id) on every opening including the first, and registers on_finished to clear each flag on {prefix}_complete *or* {prefix}_error so neither outcome can strand a spinner.

The frontend treats the _complete payload semantically: data.skipped true renders a warning toast and skips the refresh (an already-current DAT changed nothing), while a payload whose system_id equals the current selection resets system_id to the -1 sentinel because a purged system has nothing left to fetch; otherwise state.refresh() refetches what is on screen. Toast text is taken verbatim from the event's `message` field.

import_dat is the one prefix that can emit several terminal events for a single request: process_dat_upload returns a Vec<Result<ImportDatResult>> — one entry per DAT inside an uploaded ZIP — and the task sends import_dat_complete per Imported/UpToDate entry (skipped: true for the latter) or import_dat_error per failure, while ImportDatResult::Skipped (an --update against a system that does not exist) is filtered out by results.retain before the handler sees it and emits nothing at all.

shutdown_signal waits for Ctrl+C or (on unix) SIGTERM, runs optimize_database (incremental_vacuum, optimize, wal_checkpoint(truncate)) and only then calls cancel.cancel(), so /events streams stay open for the duration of the checkpoint before all terminating together. The shared token breaks every SSE receive loop and unblocks in-flight MCP actions, which race work against the per-request ctx.ct ('cancelled by the client') and self.cancel ('server shutting down'); spawned CLI actions from GraphQL mutations and uploads are not watched for cancellation and run to completion.

/events is reached same-origin in every deployment: the embedded SPA is served from the same listener, the Tauri shell spawns `oxyromon server` on an ephemeral loopback port and points the webview at that origin, and in development `trunk serve` proxies /events to http://127.0.0.1:8000/events. The route has no authentication, so it is readable by anything that can reach the bound address.

No test exercises /events or MCP progress notifications: the server tests boot the real main() and assert only HTTP status codes (202 accepted, 400 rejected) or re-query GraphQL after a sleep, and tests/mcp_stdio.rs builds tools/call params without a progressToken so the progress poller never runs under test. Its hand-rolled client reads stdout until a line carries its own id (so unsolicited notifications are tolerated) and close() asserts a clean exit on stdin EOF. Consequently the SSE event names and payload shapes are an unverified contract — renaming a prefix compiles cleanly, silently breaks the matching SPA listener, and fails no test.

The byte-level progress that ultimately reaches MCP clients comes from a workspace-wide contract: each format crate entry point takes `progress: &mut dyn FnMut(u64)` called with the input bytes consumed since the last call, adding up to the input size, and run_blocking in src/progress.rs adapts that callback to `bar.inc(n)` on a bytes-styled bar of `length` moved onto the blocking pool. Callers supply the matching total — the input file's metadata().len() for xso-rs/nsz/xdelta/xps, chd_rs::cd_input_size for a CD image, gdi_rs::input_size for GDI, and the CHD's info().logical_size when extracting — so those byte counts are precisely the position/total pair the poller forwards.

The mcp and server subcommands never enable plain output: main sets it only when the MultiProgress is hidden and the subcommand is neither mcp nor server, so server-side actions keep printing through hidden bars instead of writing to stderr.
